title: Thirteen pigeons
hook: Can you be certain two people share a birth month, without knowing anyone's birthday?

doesNotKnow: that more items than boxes guarantees a box with two (the pigeonhole principle)

misconception: Sharing a box is only ever likely, never certain, with so few items.
objective: The learner can explain that 12 people can all have different birth months, but any 13 must include two who share one, because there are only 12 months.

claims.text: There are 12 months, so 12 people can each have a different birth month.
claims.source: The Gregorian calendar has 12 months; one person per month is an arrangement with no month shared.

claims.text: Any 13 people must include two who share a birth month; 13 is the smallest number that guarantees it.
claims.source: If every month held at most one person there would be at most 12 people; 12 is not enough because of the arrangement in c1.

claims.text: More items than boxes forces some box to hold two (the pigeonhole principle).
claims.source: If n boxes held at most one item each there would be at most n items. Named Schubfachprinzip after Dirichlet (1834); e.g. Engel, Problem-Solving Strategies, ch. 4.

recall.question: A drawer holds loose socks in 3 colours. In the dark, how many socks must you take to be certain of a matching pair?
recall.why: Three socks can all be different colours, but a fourth must repeat one of the 3 colours: more socks than colours forces a pair.
